items.explain: They refuse the reserved shelter bed and curfew, staying instead between a church, the library and time with a friend.
They spend days near a sick, untested friend and will likely test positive for a lung infection if screened.
They only sometimes pick up blood pressure medication, so their blood pressure stays too high.
They unexpectedly get off the streets, either moving in with a sister or getting a council flat years later.
They try to complain about their housing with outside help, but official routing and a closure letter shut it down.
They drop out of the tenants' meetings after the time moves to clash with their care work shifts.
They keep working zero-hours care shifts on low pay, with a steadier contract possible but not promised.
Their benefits settle down and they stay on long-term antidepressants, but the depression could return at any time.

items.plain: Body forces end of care work
items.explain: Years of physical strain end their care job in their early fifties, leaving them on disability benefits in the same flat.
They use direct access to company bosses to renew accusations against a colleague's flawed forecasting system.
Their daughter moves away to university, and they mostly hear about her through their ex-partner.
They hit project deadlines while 44 jobs are cut, and receive extra pay to stay at the company.
Their drinking grows to a medically harmful level, alongside high blood pressure and insomnia treated with sleeping pills.
They settle for a lesser regional job, live alone and see their daughter only occasionally.
Their daughter, their closest bond, moves away to university, leaving the couple alone and growing apart.
They begin solo counselling on Thursday evenings, replacing some time spent in the park and a skipped couples session.
They escalate the flat's mould problem beyond the housing office, to child protection or a local councillor.
After separating, they openly partner with a work colleague and settle into a stable home life locally.
Their reduced work hours end and they return to nearly full-time teaching at the same primary school.
